questions.question: Analyse the significance of Poirot's choice to leave the final decision to M. Bouc and Dr. Constantine.
questions.solution_html:
• Poirot presents two solutions in Murder on the Orient Express to balance truth with
  • morality. The first - a mysterious stranger committed the murder - offers a simple, lawful
  • explanation. The second - all twelve passengers killed Ratchett to avenge Daisy
  • Armstrong - reveals the moral truth behind the crime. Poirot, aware that strict justice
  • would only punish those who sought to right a great wrong, gives both versions to let M.
  • Bouc and Dr. Constantine choose between legal duty and moral conscience - upholds both
  • truth and humanity, allowing justice to take a compassionate form. / [CO3]

questions.question: Evaluate “Death and the Compass” as both detective fiction and philosophical allegory.
questions.solution_html:
• Moderately lenient evaluation recommended. Borges writes “Death and the Compass”
  • as a detective story that also questions human reason. Borges begins with a detective
  • story — a murder, clues, and a clever investigator — but turns it into a reflection on
  • reason and fate. Detective Lönnrot follows logic so perfectly that it traps him and leads
  • him to death. His search for order becomes a journey into error and walks into the logical
  • labyrinth set by Scharlach. Borges uses the detective form to ask deeper questions about
  • knowledge, destiny, and the limits of reason. Borges shows that reason can become a
  • trap and that truth may lie beyond logic. What reads like a mystery becomes a meditation
  • on how our need for meaning and over-reliance on intellect can lead to destruction. Thus,
  • the story is both a mystery and a philosophical puzzle. / [CO3]

questions.question: Evaluate Freeman’s criticism of false clues in detective stories.
questions.solution_html:
• R. Austin Freeman, in “The Art of the Detective Story” criticizes the use of false clues or
  • red herrings in detective stories because they deceive the reader instead of engaging them
  • in fair reasoning. He insists that detective fiction should be based on fair play — the
  • reader must have access to all the real clues needed to solve the mystery. False clues, he
  • argues, weaken logic, create artificial suspense, and make the story depend on tricks
  • rather than intellect. Freeman believes a good writer can maintain suspense by presenting
  • true clues clearly but subtly, trusting the reader to mislead themselves through
  • misinterpretation. He sees false clues as a mark of poor technique and “bad practice”
  • because they destroy the intellectual satisfaction that defines genuine detective fiction.
  • / [CO1]
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: How does the resolution of the case highlight Poe's larger theme that imagination and psychological insight are central to true detection?
questions.solution_html:
• Lenient evaluation recommended. In “The Purloined Letter,” Dupin solves the mystery
  • by imagining how the criminal thinks. Poe shows that real detection is not just about
  • logic but about understanding the human mind. Dupin succeeds because he uses both
  • reason and imagination. The police search every corner mechanically, but Dupin realises
  • that the clever Minister D would hide the letter in the most obvious place — right in
  • front of everyone. Poe uses this moment to show that intelligence alone is not enough;
  • what matters is the ability to think creatively and to read the psychology of others. Dupin
  • succeeds because he understands pride, vanity, and the habits of the human mind. The
  • story becomes more than a puzzle — it’s about how imagination can uncover truth when
  • reason fails. / [CO2]

questions.question: How does “A Study in Pink”challenge traditional ideas of right and wrong through its characters? [15x2 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Lenient evaluation recommended. “A Study in Pink” is a modern story that changes the
  • old idea of moral certainty. Sherlock uses reason without emotion, while the killer
  • believes he is doing moral work by punishing the corrupt. Both act from belief, not pure
  • good or evil. Both follow their own rules. The cab driver kills people as part of a strange
  • and deadly game. He offers his victims two pills — one harmless and one poisoned —
  • claiming that if they choose the wrong one, it’s their fate. The story shows that truth and
  • justice are complex, and the ending doesn’t give clear justice. Holmes wins through
  • logic, but the moral result is uncertain, making viewers question what is truly right. It
  • shows that modern detective stories explore moral doubt as much as they solve crime. It
  • reveals a world where human choices are complex and morality depends on perspective
  • rather than fixed rules. / [CO3]
